USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the G20 90-day window to negotiate hard for enforceable structural commitments (IP, forced tech transfer, cyber, non-tariff barriers) plus immediate, measurable farm and energy purchases—without rolling back existing Section 301 tariffs or trading the Meng extradition case. Keep the suspended List 3 hike to 25% as the deadline incentive; do not add new tariff or entity-list actions while talks are live. Compartment the Huawei/Meng sanctions case from the trade table, and press Beijing to release the detained Canadians so the truce is not poisoned by hostage diplomacy.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is real but not high: US industrial production is still firm (INDPRO ~104.1) and Michigan sentiment remains elevated at 98.3, so this is not a recession-scale shock. The bite is concentrated and political—US goods exports to China are down ~9% in the lookback, China’s matching retaliation on soy/autos/aircraft has already cratered farm-belt demand (US soybean sales to China down ~94% through mid-October; Illinois soy prices fell ~$2.50/bu), and USDA had to stand up a $12B aid package. Markets are signaling risk (VIX 25.58 on 19 Dec, +48% in-window; 10-year yield back to 2.77 from a 3.24 peak; WTI −31%). The Dec 1 G20 pause bought time by freezing the Jan 1 List 3 hike, but there is no joint text: Washington claims a 90-day structural clock and “very substantial” immediate purchases; Beijing describes only a halt to new tariffs and gradual import increases “according to domestic needs.” Same-day arrest of Meng Wanzhou on a US Iran-sanctions warrant, followed by China’s Dec 10 detention of Kovrig and Spavor, injects a second track that could collapse talks if either side escalates. That mix is a modest threat (+0.22), not an opportunity to restructure on US terms and not an existential cascade. Action should therefore stay near zero: negotiate inside the window rather than escalate (which would hit already-stressed markets and farm constituencies) or concede (existing $250B of 301 coverage is the leverage, and China has not yet delivered matching structural offers). Second-order risk of further tariff hikes now is a Chinese walk-away plus deeper soy-market diversion to Brazil; second-order risk of premature rollback is losing the only instrument that brought Xi to the table.
key_factors: G20 90-day truce froze the Jan 1 List 3 hike to 25% but left existing ~$250B of Section 301 tariffs in place
No joint communique: US and China publicly disagree on the 90-day clock, purchase amounts, and structural agenda
Farm-belt retaliation is already material (soy sales to China ~−94%; prices down; $12B USDA aid)
US real economy still resilient (sentiment, IP) while financial conditions have tightened (VIX, falling 10Y, oil crash)
Meng Wanzhou arrest plus Kovrig/Spavor detentions create a hostage/tech-security overlay that could blow up compartmentalized trade talks
China showing more trade-flow strain (SA merchandise exports −4.5%, imports −14.9%, CNY ~+5% weaker vs USD) — US still holds unused tariff leverage

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended (tariffs remain at 10%). Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
China detains Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor (widely viewed as retaliation for the Meng arrest; Beijing denies linkage).
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
VIX latest 25.58 on 2018-12-19, change +8.25 (+47.6%) over the 180-day window — equity-vol stress after the truce/Meng news.
US goods exports to mainland China latest $9.21B (Dec), −9.3% in-window; farm/industrial shipments already shrinking under retaliation.
Michigan consumer sentiment 98.3 (Dec) — still high; real-side US demand not collapsing.
China SA merchandise exports down to $196.9B (Dec), −4.5% in-window; imports −14.9% — opponent under more trade-flow pressure than the US real economy.
White House: China to purchase a not-yet-agreed but 'very substantial' amount of ag/energy/industrial goods and start farm purchases immediately; 90-day clock or List 3 goes to 25%.
No joint statement; Chinese officials made no mention of the 90-day deadline or specific structural issues; purchases framed only as gradual easing of imbalance.
American soybean sales to China down 94% from last year's harvest through mid-October; beans stockpiled; local prices below $7 vs ~$10 a year earlier.
Meng arrest (unknown to Trump at the G20 dinner) injected new unpredictability into the 90-day talks and drew a sharp Chinese protest demanding immediate release.
